analysis.one_liner: Strips away the court-created immunity that shields state and local officials from lawsuits for violating constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: Introduced by a single Republican senator with no cosponsors, the bill was never taken up by the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: When a state or local official — most often a police officer — violates someone's constitutional rights, a Supreme Court-made doctrine called qualified immunity usually lets them off the hook unless the victim can point to a past court case with nearly identical facts. This bill would rewrite the 1871 civil rights law to say that acting in good faith or not knowing the right existed is no defense, making officials personally answerable in damages suits. It would also make municipalities financially liable for their employees' violations, while keeping a narrow protection for officers whose conduct was required by written law or already upheld by a court.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose constitutional rights are violated by state or local government employees, most often police. Today many of them lose their case in the first round of the lawsuit because the judge finds no earlier court decision with nearly identical facts. The bill would let those cases go to a jury on their merits, restoring the remedy Congress wrote into the 1871 law that has been the main tool for victims of police misconduct and other official wrongdoing.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes into the civil rights statute that acting in good faith, believing the conduct was lawful, or being unable to know the right was 'clearly established' is not a defense in a lawsuit for deprivation of rights.

It makes a municipality or other local government financially liable when its employee violates someone's rights within the scope of employment, and bars the good-faith and clearly-established defenses in those cases.

It keeps a limited shield: an individual defendant avoids liability if the conduct was specifically authorized or required by a statute or regulation, no court had struck that provision down, and the defendant reasonably believed the conduct was constitutional — or if a court had already upheld that specific conduct.

The bill's stated findings argue the Supreme Court's qualified immunity decisions have frustrated Congress's original intent in passing the 1871 Ku Klux Klan Act and left constitutional rights inadequately protected.

analysis.who_pays: Municipal and local governments and their insurers, who would face damages judgments for employee misconduct and could raise premiums or taxes to cover them. Individual officers would face personal liability in suits where no statute required their conduct and no court had approved it. Taxpayers in cities could bear higher insurance and settlement costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cities, police officers, and municipal insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not abolish official immunity entirely: an officer whose conduct was required by written law, or that a court had already upheld, still escapes personal liability, so some victims would still lose on this defense.

Imposing liability on municipalities for employee misconduct raises direct costs for local governments, which could translate into higher insurance premiums and settlements paid out of local budgets that taxpayers fund.
The bill addresses only suits against state and local officials under section 1983; it does not create a parallel remedy for violations by federal officers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the bill's benefit is concrete: a person wrongfully beaten, searched, or jailed by a local official could get a real damages case instead of losing on a technicality of court-made law. The costs are real but ordinary features of any liability regime — governments and insurers pay claims, and defensive behavior by officers. The carve-out for conduct required by statute blunts the harshest concerns while leaving the core reform intact.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate on June 23, 2020, sent to the Judiciary Committee, never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor, and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Braun of Indiana, a Republican, introduced the Reforming Qualified Immunity Act in the Senate on June 23, 2020.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, where no further action was taken — no hearing, markup, or vote.
No senator from either party cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list shows zero cosponsors.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died in committee without reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local government employees, especially police, and the municipalities that employ them: because the bill died, the Supreme Court's qualified immunity doctrine remains fully in place, and victims of rights violations continue to be screened out of court unless they can cite a nearly identical past case. Cities and their insurers also avoided the new municipal liability the bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officials shielded by the status quo

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Reforming Qualified Immunity Act and became its sole sponsor; no senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee where the bill was referred, took no action on it — no hearing or markup was scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: Law enforcement organizations
against.role: Police unions and associations active in the 2020 qualified-immunity debate
against.what_they_did: Were widely reported to have lobbied Congress and the White House against ending or limiting qualified immunity during the 2020 policing debate.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican, but no senator of either party cosponsored the bill and no vote ever occurred, so the partisan split on this bill was never tested — even though qualified-immunity reform drew interest from both parties during 2020.

industries.industry: State and local government employees, especially police
industries.note: The bill would strip the good-faith and clearly-established defenses that let officials avoid personal damages liability for violating rights, though a carve-out protects those acting under written law or court-approved conduct. That liability exposure is exactly what lets victims obtain compensation, so the interest runs against the public's.

The bill makes municipalities directly liable for employee rights violations within the scope of employment and bars them from raising the officer's good faith as a defense. Cities would pay more in judgments and settlements, costs ultimately borne by local taxpayers.
Insurers would face more claims from cities but could offset this with higher premiums charged to local governments, which taxpayers fund. Either way the bill's death left them with the status quo.
